Fake Microsoft Alerts Used to Deploy North Korean NarwhalRAT Malware

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The North Korean state-sponsored hacking group known as ScarCruft (aka APT37) has been observed using spear-phishing messages impersonating Microsoft Account security notifications to deliver a new malware called NarwhalRAT. "The attack email contained a message impersonating an MS account security alert," the Genians Security Center (GSC) said. "It was designed to create concern over possible

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ScarCruft fake Microsoft Account 'OTP abuse' alert with ZIP attachment · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT in-memory loader: python.exe processing a Windows CAT file · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] LNK from extracted ZIP spawning batch script that downloads Python and CAT file · [LLM] Scheduled task creation with NarwhalRAT 'Microsoft*TaskMachine' naming convention · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT C2 to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr / pCloud dead-drop with folderid+auth · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NarwhalRAT staging directory %APPDATA%\naverwhale (Naver Whale browser masquerade) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ScarCruft fake Microsoft Account 'OTP abuse' alert with ZIP attachment AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound spear-phishing emails impersonating Microsoft Account security notifications about repeated OTP generation / abnormal activity, with a ZIP attachment that conceals a malicious LNK file. This is the article-specific NarwhalRAT initial-access lure. Rationale: Uses article's exact lure pattern (impersonated MS Account security alert about repeated OTP generation / abnormal activity) combined with the specific ZIP-containing-LNK delivery shape. Genians' report is the primary source; no second source needed because IOCs were taken directly from the named research org. Sentinel left empty because the listed Sentinel tenant schema in this prompt does not include EmailEvents / EmailAttachmentInfo — inbound mail phishing visibility for this tenant is Defender XDR only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1598.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Microsoft account security notifications spoofed via lookalike domains used in phishing tests
  • Internal IT security awareness training emails containing simulated MS-account lures
  • Bug bounty / external researcher submissions referencing OTP abuse in subject line
  • Third-party SSO partners sending password-rotation reminders that mention 'Microsoft account'
Suppression filter
| where not(SenderFromAddress in~ ("security-noreply@microsoft.com", "account-security-noreply@accountprotection.microsoft.com")) and not(Subject has "phishing simulation")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the EmailAttachmentInfo SHA256 of the ZIP and any LNK contained within; check VirusTotal and abuse.ch for the hash; pivot on RecipientEmailAddress to confirm whether the recipient opened the attachment (DeviceFileEvents extraction of the LNK; DeviceProcessEvents for explorer.exe spawning cmd/powershell shortly after). 2) Contain: block SenderFromAddress and SenderFromDomain at the connector; recall the message tenant-wide via Quarantine and Soft Delete; isolate any device that extracted the LNK. 3) Hunt: across the tenant, look for any inbound mail in the last 30 days from the same sender domain, any other recipients of the same SHA256 attachment, and downstream IOCs (process tree from LNK execution, connections to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr, scheduled tasks named 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine' or 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine').
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where Subject has_any ("Microsoft account", "security alert", "OTP", "one-time password", "abnormal activity", "password")
| where not(SenderFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com") and not(SenderMailFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".zip"
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256, FileSize
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, AttachmentSHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where Subject has_any ("Microsoft account", "security alert", "OTP", "one-time password", "abnormal activity", "password")
| where not(SenderFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com") and not(SenderMailFromDomain endswith "microsoft.com")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".zip"
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256, FileSize
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, AttachmentSHA256, FileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Inbound Microsoft Account Security Alert Lure with ZIP Attachment
id: 5b0e8e8c-6d5b-4c2d-9e2c-2c1d8e8f5a01
description: Detects ScarCruft NarwhalRAT delivery pattern - email impersonating Microsoft Account security alert with ZIP attachment that contains a LNK file.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1566.001
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: email
  product: microsoft365
detection:
  selection_subject:
    Subject|contains:
      - 'Microsoft account'
      - 'security alert'
      - 'OTP'
      - 'one-time password'
      - 'abnormal activity'
  selection_attachment:
    AttachmentName|endswith: '.zip'
  filter_legit:
    SenderFromDomain|endswith: 'microsoft.com'
  condition: all of selection_* and not filter_legit
level: high
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.action="delivered" All_Email.file_name="*.zip" (All_Email.subject="*Microsoft account*" OR All_Email.subject="*security alert*" OR All_Email.subject="*OTP*" OR All_Email.subject="*one-time password*" OR All_Email.subject="*abnormal activity*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name All_Email.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | where NOT match(src_user, "(?i)@microsoft\.com$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Email.All_Email where All_Email.action="delivered" All_Email.file_name="*.zip" (All_Email.subject="*Microsoft account*" OR All_Email.subject="*security alert*" OR All_Email.subject="*OTP*" OR All_Email.subject="*one-time password*" OR All_Email.subject="*abnormal activity*") by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient All_Email.subject All_Email.file_name All_Email.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | where NOT match(src_user, "(?i)@microsoft\.com$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
LNK from extracted ZIP spawning batch script that downloads Python and CAT file AIInstallation High
Detects the NarwhalRAT loader chain: an LNK file (extracted from a phishing ZIP) launches cmd.exe to run a batch script that uses curl/bitsadmin/powershell to fetch the legitimate Python installer plus a malicious Windows security catalog (.cat) file from attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Article explicitly describes the chain LNK -> batch script -> downloads Python + CAT file. Combines explorer.exe-spawned shell parent (the only way an extracted-from-ZIP LNK can launch) with downloader keywords and article's exact second-stage indicators (.cat, Python download). Cross-referenced with Genians GSC public IOC bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin running ad-hoc cmd.exe scripts from a desktop shortcut that uses curl for legitimate downloads
  • Developer LNK shortcuts to .bat build scripts that call python.exe
  • Software installer LNKs that invoke bitsadmin for first-run updates
  • Help-desk troubleshooting LNKs that invoke Invoke-WebRequest to fetch diagnostic tooling
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm", "intune", "chocolatey", "winget")) and not(AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the LNK target via DeviceFileEvents (look for InitiatingProcessFileName='explorer.exe' and FileName endswith '.lnk' within minutes prior); pull SHA256 and check against IOC list (3715092a..., 7cef19f9..., 7eb9cee1..., b6b06023...). 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response; kill the cmd/powershell tree and any python.exe child; remove the scheduled task if already created. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent ZIP - find EmailAttachmentInfo for the SHA256 of the ZIP, identify all recipients tenant-wide, look for the staging folder %APPDATA%\naverwhale, look for outbound connections to daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, fe01.co.kr, and the IPs 121.254.222.10/80, 211.239.157.126, 218.150.78.198/231, 61.100.9.206.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".lnk", ".bat")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl", "bitsadmin", "Invoke-WebRequest", "python", ".cat", "daehoat", "novel21", "fe01.co.kr")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (".lnk", ".bat") or CommandLine has_any ("curl", "bitsadmin", "Invoke-WebRequest", "python", ".cat", "daehoat", "novel21", "fe01.co.kr")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: LNK Extracted From Phishing ZIP Spawns Loader Batch Script
id: 7e4d3a9c-1f2b-4a8e-9c11-3a5b1c2d8f02
description: Detects NarwhalRAT loader chain where explorer.exe-spawned cmd/powershell from an LNK invokes curl/bitsadmin/python plus a .cat fetch.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  selection_indicators:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.lnk'
      - '.bat'
      - 'curl'
      - 'bitsadmin'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'python'
      - '.cat'
      - 'daehoat'
      - 'novel21'
      - 'fe01.co.kr'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.exe OR *\EXPLORER.EXE) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe) @CommandLine:(*lnk* OR *bat* OR *curl* OR *bitsadmin* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *python* OR *.cat* OR *daehoat* OR *novel21* OR *fe01.co.kr*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(\\.lnk|\\.bat|curl|bitsadmin|Invoke-WebRequest|python|\\.cat|daehoat|novel21|fe01\\.co\\.kr)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.bat*") (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*bitsadmin*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*python*" OR Processes.process="*.cat*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.parent_process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.lnk*" OR Processes.process="*.bat*") (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*bitsadmin*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*python*" OR Processes.process="*.cat*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Scheduled task creation with NarwhalRAT 'Microsoft*TaskMachine' naming convention AIInstallation High
Detects creation of scheduled tasks whose names follow the ScarCruft NarwhalRAT convention: 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine' or 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine'. Naming convention shared across multiple Python-based ScarCruft campaigns - tasks launch the CAT file that pulls and in-memory loads the main payload. Rationale: Article gives two literal task names ('MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine', 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine'); both are distinct enough that combined with schtasks.exe /create they are near zero-FP. Note 'TackMachine' is not a typo - the article explicitly preserves that naming. Also checks the on-disk task XML drop in %WINDIR%\System32\Tasks\ as a second pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager (MECM/SCCM) deploying scheduled tasks with 'Microsoft' prefixes via custom packages
  • Microsoft Office click-to-run telemetry tasks created during MSI install
  • Internal IT scripted task creation using 'MicrosoftUpdates' or similar prefix conventions
  • Windows Update Medic Service (WaaSMedicSvc) creating Microsoft-prefixed remediation tasks
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe", "tiworker.exe", "officeclicktorun.exe", "setup.exe", "msiexec.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the XML body of the matching task from %WINDIR%\System32\Tasks\<name> via Defender Live Response; identify the action (typically launches the .cat file via cmd or powershell). 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task (schtasks /delete /tn <name> /f), kill any running children, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: across the estate look for any other Microsoft-prefixed tasks created in the same 7-day window from non-MECM parents; pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName to find the loader; look for in-memory python.exe processes and outbound traffic to article IOCs (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, pCloud).
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\System32\Tasks\"
  | where FileName has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
  | where CommandLine has "/create"
  | where CommandLine has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
),
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4698
  | where EventData has_any ("MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures", "MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage", "TaskMachine", "TackMachine")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventID, EventData
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ScarCruft NarwhalRAT Scheduled Task Naming Pattern
id: a1f7b2d8-9c4e-4e8b-bf01-3d2c8a9b5e03
description: Detects creation of scheduled task with the ScarCruft NarwhalRAT naming convention (MicrosoftUserInterfacePicturesUpdateTackMachine, MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackageTaskMachine).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_bin:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_create:
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  selection_name:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures'
      - 'MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage'
      - 'TaskMachine'
      - 'TackMachine'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/create* AND (*MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures* OR *MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage* OR *TaskMachine* OR *TackMachine*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)\\/create", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures|MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage|TaskMachine|TackMachine)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*Microsoft*TaskMachine*" OR Processes.process="*Microsoft*TackMachine*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*Microsoft*TaskMachine*" OR Processes.process="*Microsoft*TackMachine*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftUserInterfacePictures*" OR Processes.process="*MicrosoftMusicLibrariesPackage*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
NarwhalRAT in-memory loader: python.exe processing a Windows CAT file AIExploitation High
Detects the article-specific in-memory execution structure where the legitimate Python interpreter (downloaded from python.org) is launched with a Windows security catalog (.cat) file as input - the CAT is repurposed as a Python script container so the main payload runs in memory without disk artifacts. Rationale: Article: 'launch the CAT file responsible for fetching and running the main payload in memory without leaving any artifacts on disk' and 'Python-based multi-stage loader, an in-memory execution structure'. Combination python.exe + .cat extension is anomalous (CAT files are normally consumed by Windows code signing / WinVerifyTrust, not Python). Very rare benign hits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python developers genuinely processing certificate trust list files for code-signing tooling research
  • Antivirus signature-development workflow scripts that diff catalog files
  • Internal red-team education modules demonstrating LOLBin script abuse
  • Custom Microsoft Update validation tooling that wraps signtool/makecat with python wrappers
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared", @"\Windows\System32\CatRoot"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the .cat path - if it sits in %APPDATA%, %TEMP%, %PUBLIC%, or %APPDATA%\naverwhale this is highly likely malicious; pull the file hash and content sample via Defender Live Response. 2) Contain: kill the python.exe tree, isolate host, capture memory dump for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same python.exe ProcessId to find C2 (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, pCloud); look for the scheduled task that launched the chain; sweep estate for any other python.exe + .cat combinations in the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "python.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".cat" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".cat"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "python.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "python.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".cat"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: python.exe Loading a Windows CAT File (NarwhalRAT Loader)
id: 8b3c9f1a-6d2e-4a5c-9012-4e6d2f3a8b04
description: Detects the legitimate Python interpreter invoked with a .cat file argument - ScarCruft NarwhalRAT uses this to hide an in-memory payload inside a Windows security catalog file extension.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-microsoft-alerts-used-to-deploy.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:

  - attack.t1027
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_python:
    Image|endswith: '\python.exe'
  selection_cat:
    CommandLine|contains: '.cat'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE) @CommandLine:*.cat*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/python\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)\\.cat", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="python.exe" Processes.process="*.cat*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="python.exe" Processes.process="*.cat*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
NarwhalRAT staging directory %APPDATA%\naverwhale (Naver Whale browser masquerade) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation, write, or process activity referencing the article's distinctive staging directory %APPDATA%\naverwhale, which NarwhalRAT uses to stage harvested keylogger output, screenshots, audio recordings, and USB media before exfil. Name masquerades as the South Korean Naver Whale browser. Rationale: Article explicitly: 'The moniker NarwhalRAT is a reference to the malware's use of %APPDATA%\naverwhale to stage the harvested information' and the name masquerades as Naver Whale. Path string is unique enough to be near-zero FP because the legitimate Naver Whale browser uses '%LOCALAPPDATA%\Naver\Naver Whale' (different parent, different casing, space, different folder) - the 'naverwhale' (one word, no space, in Roaming) is the article's distinctive IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1074.001 T1056.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Korean-speaking developers writing tooling that programmatically references a folder literally called 'naverwhale' for legitimate research
  • Naver Whale browser uninstaller leaving residual breadcrumbs under Roaming during cleanup
  • Internal threat-intel team running detonation/IOC validation against the article's path on a sandbox machine
  • Security researchers writing test cases that drop files into the same path
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("whale.exe", "naver_whale.exe", "WhaleUpdate.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate contents of %APPDATA%\naverwhale via Live Response - expect keylog dumps, screenshots, audio captures; pull file metadata. 2) Contain: isolate device, kill python.exe process(es) writing to the path, snapshot the folder before purging for forensic preservation. 3) Hunt: across all hosts grep DeviceFileEvents for any FolderPath has 'naverwhale'; pivot the writing process backwards through process tree to confirm Python loader chain; check DeviceNetworkEvents for exfil to daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr, pCloud API endpoints.
union
(
  DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ActionType="ProcessRef", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\naverwhale"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NarwhalRAT Staging Directory naverwhale Under AppData
id: 2c7e1b4a-3f5d-4b8c-a201-5f7e2d3a9c05

NarwhalRAT C2 to daehoat.com / novel21.co.kr / pCloud dead-drop with folderid+auth AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound C2 traffic to ScarCruft NarwhalRAT primary relays (daehoat.com, novel21.co.kr) and secondary pCloud-based dead-drop resolver - identifies pCloud abuse via the article-specific URL parameter combination 'folderid' + 'auth' which the malware uses to fetch staged commands. Rationale: Article names two primary C2 relays ('daehoat[.]com' and 'novel21[.]co.kr') plus the pCloud API dead-drop resolver pattern with folderid+auth params; pre-extracted IOC bundle adds three more Korean-hosted domains and six IPs. Multiple-table union covers EDR network telemetry plus proxy/firewall (CEF/CommonSecurityLog) and DNS — common SOC visibility gaps in different orgs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.genians.co.kr/en/blog/threat_intelligence/narwhal-rat • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Korean-speaking employees legitimately browsing daehoat.com (a real Korean-hosted site) or novel21.co.kr literary websites
  • Backup/sync clients of pCloud users in the org transferring folderid+auth normally — normal pCloud client UI does use those params
  • Threat-intel team detonating samples in production network without isolation
  • Public proxy / Tor exit nodes that happen to share one of the listed IPs
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pcloud.exe", "pcloud-sync.exe", "chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "whale.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on InitiatingProcessFileName - if python.exe or schtasks-spawned cmd.exe is the initiator on a non-Korea-business host, escalate to incident; check whether the device also shows %APPDATA%\naverwhale. 2) Contain: block IPs and domains at perimeter and EDR network containment; isolate the host; capture memory. 3) Hunt: 30-day backtrack across all hosts for any of the six listed IPs and five domains; check Email egress for any messages to recipients matching the same actor pattern; for pCloud, look for any other python.exe processes making pCloud API calls with folderid+auth - those are the dead-drop fetch routines.
union
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("daehoat.com", "novel21.co.kr", "fe01.co.kr", "crwellfood.com", "webhostingkorea.com")
     or RemoteIP in ("121.254.222.10", "121.254.222.80", "211.239.157.126", "218.150.78.198", "218.150.78.231", "61.100.9.206")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
),
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has "api.pcloud.com" or RemoteUrl has "eapi.pcloud.com"
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("folderid", "naverwhale")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any ("daehoat.com", "novel21.co.kr", "fe01.co.kr", "crwellfood.com", "webhostingkorea.com")
     or RequestURL has_any ("daehoat.com", "novel21.co.kr", "fe01.co.kr")
     or DestinationIP in ("121.254.222.10", "121.254.222.80", "211.239.157.126", "218.150.78.198", "218.150.78.231", "61.100.9.206")
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceProduct
),
(
  DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has_any ("daehoat.com", "novel21.co.kr", "fe01.co.kr", "crwellfood.com", "webhostingkorea.com")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
),
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where HttpHostName has "pcloud.com"
  | where Url has "folderid" and Url has "auth"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or SHA1 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or MD5 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or SHA1 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b") or MD5 in~ ("3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3715092aa00f380cefe8b4d2eddb7d08", "7cef19f9c4480adac0cd4702ff98f46c", "7eb9cee1f696727752169f25cf79a338", "b6b0602310bb2d4360c52685119aac1b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Releases Security Updates for Actively Exploited SD-WAN Manager Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 7 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cisco has released security updates for a medium-severity security flaw in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager that has come under active exploitation in the wild. vManage SdraAnyConnect handler writes WAR via path traversal AIExploitation High
Hunts for the CVE-2026-20262 exploitation signal in vmanage-server.log — the AnyConnect file-upload handler logging an 'uploaded Remote Access Anyconnect profile file' record whose destination path contains '../' or lands a .war/.jsp in the Wildfly deployments folder. Legitimate AnyConnect profile uploads never traverse path, so this is the high-fidelity arbitrary-file-write primitive. Rationale: Anchored on the exact log line from the Cisco advisory body: 'SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler ... uploaded Remote Access Anyconnect profile file: ../../../../var/lib/wildfly/standalone/deployments/suspicious.war'. The combination of the handler name + literal action string + a traversal sequence in the destination is uniquely associated with CVE-2026-20262 exploitation. Cross-checked against the Cisco PSIRT advisory and BleepingComputer write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-arbfw-c2rZvQ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisco-fixes-sd-wan-vmanage-flaw-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cisco-sd-wan-vmanage-vulnerability-exploit/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco TAC-guided diagnostic upload that intentionally crafts a path traversal for debugging (rare, planned)
  • Internal red-team or PSIRT-led pen test against the vManage cluster
  • Legacy AnyConnect XML profile naming that includes a '..' literal in the filename but not as a traversal (unlikely — vManage strips these)
  • Backup/restore tooling staging WAR/JSP files via the AnyConnect API endpoint (non-standard, vendor-supported tooling uses different endpoints)
Suppression filter
and not (UploadedPath matches regex @"^/var/lib/cisco/profiles/[a-z0-9_-]+\.xml$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full vmanage-server.log record + 5-min window around it. Capture the session id from the bracket prefix (e.g. a66cdc5f-807d-4c23-944e-5c809a2ece6b), the authenticated username, source IP from the vManage audit log. 2) Contain: snapshot the appliance, remove the dropped artefact from /var/lib/wildfly/standalone/deployments/, disable the suspected admin account, isolate the vManage from edge routers if cluster-managed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same session id and source IP in vmanage-appserver.log for WFLYSRV0010 deployments and in serviceproxy-access.log for POSTs to the deployed JSP path; check for lateral pivots to controller/validator nodes; review NMS audit log for policy changes by the same user.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler"
| where SyslogMessage has "uploaded Remote Access Anyconnect profile file"
| extend UploadedPath = extract(@"file:\s+(\S+)\s+to\s+vManage", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where UploadedPath has "../" or UploadedPath endswith ".war" or UploadedPath endswith ".jsp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, UploadedPath, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cisco vManage AnyConnect Upload Handler Path Traversal (CVE-2026-20262)
id: 6f4a8e21-1c2d-4a9f-9b21-3e8c5d7f1234
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-20262 via path traversal in the SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler — arbitrary file write into the Wildfly deployments directory.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisco-releases-security-updates-for.html
  - https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-arbfw-c2rZvQ
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  product: cisco_sdwan
  service: vmanage_server
detection:
  selection:
    Message|contains|all:
      - 'SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler'
      - 'uploaded Remote Access Anyconnect profile file'
      - '../'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - None known — legitimate AnyConnect profile uploads do not traverse path.
level: high
source:cisco.sdwan "SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler" "uploaded Remote Access Anyconnect profile file" "../"
APPLICATION
search index=cisco_sdwan source="/var/log/nms/vmanage-server.log" "SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler" "uploaded Remote Access Anyconnect profile file"
| rex field=_raw "file:\s+(?<uploaded_path>\S+)\s+to\s+vManage"
| where like(uploaded_path, "%../%") OR like(uploaded_path, "%.war") OR like(uploaded_path, "%.jsp")
| stats min(_time) as first_seen, count, values(uploaded_path) as paths by host
| where first_seen >= relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
Wildfly WFLYSRV0010 deploys non-baseline WAR on vManage AIInstallation High
Detects Wildfly auto-deploying a WAR file whose name is not part of the vManage baseline package set. The CVE-2026-20262 exploit drops a WAR into /var/lib/wildfly/standalone/deployments/ which Wildfly then auto-loads — surfacing as a WFLYSRV0010 'Deployed' record in vmanage-appserver.log for an unknown WAR name. Rationale: Pinned to the exact Wildfly log signature from the article: 'WFLYSRV0010: Deployed "suspicious.war" (runtime-name : "suspicious.war")'. Baseline allow-list derived from the standard vManage package set documented in Cisco's SD-WAN admin guide. Any WAR outside that list deployed at runtime is suspicious. Cross-checked Cisco PSIRT advisory which lists the same appserver log as the IOC source. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-arbfw-c2rZvQ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisco-fixes-sd-wan-vmanage-flaw-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco-released SD-WAN version upgrade introducing a new bundled WAR (e.g. a new statistics or analytics module) — coincides with a Cisco package install record
  • Cisco TAC engineer staging a diagnostic WAR for troubleshooting
  • Customer-developed add-on WAR deployed via a vendor-supported customisation channel (rare, enterprise-only)
  • Mid-upgrade transient state where the same baseline WAR is redeployed under a hot-patch suffix (e.g. vmanage-20.15.4.5.war)
Suppression filter
and not (WarName startswith "sdwan-" and WarName endswith "-hotpatch.war")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the WAR filename, deployment timestamp, and the runtime-name from the WFLYSRV0010 line. SSH (or vshell) to the vManage and hash /var/lib/wildfly/standalone/deployments/<war>; pull the .deployed marker file. 2) Contain: undeploy the WAR via 'rm -f /var/lib/wildfly/standalone/deployments/<war>.deployed' to trigger Wildfly undeploy, snapshot the appliance, rotate credentials for the user whose session uploaded it (correlate via vmanage-server.log SdraAnyConnectFileUploadHandler line in the same session-id). 3) Hunt: enumerate ALL deployed WARs across the entire vManage cluster, search serviceproxy-access.log for any POST traffic to the suspicious WAR's context root, sweep edge routers for unauthorized policy/template pushes originating from this vManage in the post-deploy window.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "WFLYSRV0010" and SyslogMessage has "Deployed"
| extend WarName = extract(@"WFLYSRV0010:\s+Deployed\s+.(\S+?\.war)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(WarName)
| where not(WarName matches regex @"^(vmanage|configuration|olap|scheduler|statistics|sdwan).*\.war$")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Count = count(), WarFiles = make_set(WarName) by Computer
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Wildfly Deploys Non-Baseline WAR on Cisco vManage (CVE-2026-20262)
id: 7a5b9f32-2d3e-5ba0-ac32-4f9d6e8a2345
description: Detects Wildfly WFLYSRV0010 auto-deployment of a WAR not part of the vManage baseline package set — indicates a web-shell drop after CVE-2026-20262 file-write exploitation.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisco-releases-security-updates-for.html
  - https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-arbfw-c2rZvQ
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  product: cisco_sdwan
  service: vmanage_appserver
detection:
  selection:
    Message|contains: 'WFLYSRV0010: Deployed'
  filter_baseline:
    Message|contains:
      - 'vmanage.war'
      - 'configuration.war'
      - 'olap.war'
      - 'scheduler.war'
      - 'statistics-app.war'
      - 'sdwan-portal.war'
  condition: selection and not filter_baseline
falsepositives:
  - Cisco-pushed package update introducing a new WAR (rare, coincides with version bump)
level: high
source:cisco.sdwan "WFLYSRV0010: Deployed" -"vmanage.war" -"configuration.war" -"olap.war" -"scheduler.war" -"statistics-app.war" -"sdwan-portal.war"
APPLICATION
search index=cisco_sdwan source="/var/log/nms/vmanage-appserver.log" "WFLYSRV0010: Deployed"
| rex field=_raw "WFLYSRV0010:\s+Deployed\s+.(?<war_name>\S+?\.war)"
| where isnotnull(war_name) AND NOT match(war_name, "^(vmanage|configuration|olap|scheduler|statistics|sdwan).*\.war$")
| stats min(_time) as first_seen, count, values(war_name) as war_files by host
| where first_seen >= relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
vManage service-proxy POST to attacker-deployed JSP webshell AICommand & Control High
Detects POST requests landing on a JSP path served by the vManage service-proxy that is not part of the legitimate vManage application context. After CVE-2026-20262 exploitation drops a WAR and Wildfly deploys it, the attacker interacts with index.jsp via HTTP POST through service-proxy — surfacing as a serviceproxy-access.log entry referencing the rogue context root. Rationale: Anchored on the literal access-log shape from the article: '"POST /suspicious/index.jsp HTTP/1.1" 200'. The vManage application context roots are well-known (login, app, portal, home, dataservice) and any POST to a JSP outside that set indicates an attacker-deployed web shell. Joining this UC with the WFLYSRV0010 'Deployed' UC by the same context root gives a deterministic exploit-to-interaction signal. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-arbfw-c2rZvQ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cisco-sd-wan-vmanage-vulnerability-exploit/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco SD-WAN upgrade introducing a new context root containing legitimate JSP endpoints (catch via version-correlated allowlist update)
  • Customer-deployed custom dashboard WAR with its own JSP (rare; would be tracked via change-management)
  • Penetration test or red-team exercise against the vManage by an authorised engagement
  • Misconfigured WAF/loadbalancer health check that probes a non-standard JSP path with a POST
Suppression filter
and not (UriPath matches regex @"^/(?:dataservice|management)/[a-z0-9_/-]+/[a-z0-9_-]+\.jsp$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the JSP path, source IP, and request-id from the access log; correlate the same request-id back to vmanage-appserver.log to find which WAR served the request; pull the response status and bytes. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the edge firewall, undeploy the offending WAR (rm /var/lib/wildfly/standalone/deployments/<war>.deployed), snapshot the appliance, rotate vManage admin and netadmin credentials, force re-onboarding of any edge router whose template was modified in the same window. 3) Hunt: pivot on source IP across all vManage cluster nodes, search for outbound connections initiated by the wildfly java process to non-management IPs (vmanage normally only talks to controllers/validators), review NMS audit log for any template/policy push by the compromised session.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "POST" and SyslogMessage has ".jsp"
| extend UriPath = extract(@"POST\s+(/\S+\.jsp)\s+HTTP", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(UriPath)
| where not(UriPath matches regex @"^/(login|app|portal|home|static|dataservice)/")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Count = count(), JspPaths = make_set(UriPath) by Computer
| order by FirstSeen desc

2026-06-16 5 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-54420 (CVSS score: 8.5), which has been described as a case of privilege

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-54420 LiteSpeed cPanel exploit: generateEcCert chained to packageUserSize for same user · [LLM] CVE-2026-54420 LiteSpeed cPanel exploit: burst of 7-10 concurrent generateEcCert / packageUserSize calls

CVE-2026-54420 LiteSpeed cPanel exploit: generateEcCert chained to packageUserSize for same user AIExploitation High
Detects the specific exploitation pattern for CVE-2026-54420 where an attacker with FTP/web shell access on a CloudLinux/CageFS shared host invokes the cPanel JSON API function `generateEcCert` immediately followed by `packageUserSize` for the same cPanel user within seconds. LiteSpeed explicitly states legitimate UI flows never chain these two calls — this is the highest-fidelity signature published by the vendor. Rationale: Anchored on the EXACT IOC strings published by LiteSpeed in the article body (`cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert`, `cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize`, `cert_action_entry.*geneccert`) and the vendor's explicit statement that legitimate UI flows never chain these two calls for the same user. The 10-second correlation window is generous; LiteSpeed says the calls are 'immediately' chained, so most true positives will be sub-second. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54420
ATT&CKT1068 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosting provider's own automation tool (e.g. WHM bulk-provisioning script) that legitimately issues both API calls for the same user during account setup
  • Custom reseller tooling that wraps cPanel API for SSL cert provisioning and disk-quota reporting in one workflow
  • Load-testing or QA suite hammering both API endpoints
  • Migration utility (e.g. transfer_tool) that batches per-user operations
  • cPanel auto-renewal cron job if it has been customised to also report user disk usage in the same flow
Suppression filter
| where User !in~ ("root", "cpanel", "nobody") and User !startswith "_" // exclude system-context calls
| where SrcIp !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") // exclude localhost (WHM UI proxies through loopback in some configs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the offending log lines via the LiteSpeed grep command on the affected server and confirm the chain is for ONE cPanel user (legitimate concurrent admin work would span many). Check `whoami`/`id` history and recent root-owned file creations under /home/<user>. 2) Contain: Immediately upgrade the LiteSpeed WHM Plugin to v5.3.2.1+ (bundles cPanel plugin v2.4.8). If patching is blocked, suspend the implicated cPanel user account and any FTP credentials. Snapshot the box for forensics before remediation. 3) Hunt: Search for new root-owned binaries, modified /etc/passwd or /etc/sudoers, new SSH keys in /root/.ssh, and outbound C2 from the host since the first observation. Pivot on SrcIp across other tenants of the shared host.
// Defender XDR does not natively ingest cPanel access logs. This query targets MDE-for-Linux hosts where cPanel logs are forwarded into /var/log via rsyslog and surfaced through DeviceEvents AdditionalFields, OR detects an admin running the LiteSpeed verification grep on a potentially-compromised server.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceName has_any ("cpanel","whm","cloudlinux") or FolderPath has "/usr/local/cpanel/"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("grep","cpanel_jsonapi_func") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("generateEcCert","packageUserSize","geneccert")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 1d;
let WindowSec = 10;
let GenCalls = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where SyslogMessage has "cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert"
    | extend User = coalesce(extract(@"cpanel_jsonapi_user=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage), extract(@"cpanel_jsonuser=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage), extract(@"\suser=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage))
    | extend SrcIp = extract(@"((?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | project GenTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, User, SrcIp, GenMsg = SyslogMessage;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize"
| extend User = coalesce(extract(@"cpanel_jsonapi_user=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage), extract(@"cpanel_jsonuser=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage), extract(@"\suser=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage))
| join kind=inner GenCalls on Computer, User
| where TimeGenerated between (GenTime .. GenTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, GenTime)
| project FirstCall_generateEcCert = GenTime, SecondCall_packageUserSize = TimeGenerated, DelaySec, Computer, User, SrcIp, GenMsg, PackageMsg = SyslogMessage
| order by FirstCall_generateEcCert desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:cpanel* OR @host:(*cpanel* OR *whm*)) ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert" OR "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize" OR "cert_action_entry" "geneccert")
#event_simpleName=/^(ProcessRollup2|SyntheticProcessRollup2)$/ | (ImageFileName=/cpanel/i OR ParentBaseFileName=/cpanel/i OR CommandLine=/cpanel_jsonapi_func=(generateEcCert|packageUserSize)/i OR CommandLine=/cert_action_entry.*geneccert/i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count()) | count > 0

| transaction dest user maxspan=10s mvlist=t

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval api_func=case(like(uri_query,"%generateEcCert%"),"generateEcCert",like(uri_query,"%packageUserSize%"),"packageUserSize",like(uri_query,"%geneccert%"),"cert_action_entry_geneccert")
| transaction dest user maxspan=10s mvlist=t
| where mvcount(api_func)>=2 AND mvfind(api_func,"generateEcCert")>=0 AND mvfind(api_func,"packageUserSize")>=0
| eval delay_sec=duration
| table _time dest src user delay_sec api_func urls
CVE-2026-54420 LiteSpeed cPanel exploit: burst of 7-10 concurrent generateEcCert / packageUserSize calls AIExploitation High
Detects the second IOC LiteSpeed published for CVE-2026-54420 exploitation: 7-10 concurrent calls to the vulnerable cPanel JSON API functions per exploitation attempt. The legitimate UI invokes these one at a time, so a sudden burst from a single source IP or for a single cPanel user is the exploit's race-condition trigger. Rationale: Anchored on LiteSpeed's second published IOC in the article: '7-10 concurrent calls per attempt (legitimate UI does one at a time)'. The 5-second bucket plus the 7-20 lower/upper bound directly encodes the vendor's stated exploit signature — tight enough to avoid normal cPanel UI flows, wide enough to catch attempts that issue slightly more or fewer parallel calls. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54420
ATT&CKT1068 T1499.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bulk SSL certificate renewal job (e.g. Let's Encrypt sweep across many cPanel users) hitting the same WHM server in parallel
  • Reseller migration tool issuing parallel API calls during a tenant transfer
  • Load test or synthetic monitoring against the WHM API
  • cPanel high-availability replication tooling that fans out per-user calls
  • Pen-test or vulnerability-scanner sweep replaying the published PoC against the box
Suppression filter
| where User != "" and User !in~ ("root", "cpanel", "nobody", "system") // exclude background system jobs
| where DistinctApis >= 1 // at least one of the two functions was hit
| where SrcIp != "127.0.0.1" // exclude localhost (WHM UI loopback)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether the concurrent calls are for ONE cPanel user (exploit) or many users (likely bulk-renewal cron). Cross-reference SrcIp with known WHM admin IPs; check for the same SrcIp also hitting `generateEcCert` followed by `packageUserSize` (UC #1) for a higher-fidelity confirm. 2) Contain: Upgrade LiteSpeed WHM Plugin to v5.3.2.1+ immediately (CISA deadline is 2026-06-18). If unable to patch, block the offending SrcIp at the perimeter and suspend the implicated cPanel user pending review. 3) Hunt: Look for root-owned artefacts created in user home directories post-burst, new SUID binaries, modifications to /etc/cron.d/, and unexpected symlinks under /home/*/public_html pointing outside CageFS. Sweep all cPanel users for FTP credentials that may have been used as the initial foothold.
// Defender XDR does not ingest cPanel access logs. This query hunts MDE-for-Linux hosts where cPanel JSON API calls leak into DeviceEvents AdditionalFields via syslog forwarding, or detects the LiteSpeed verification grep being executed.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AdditionalFields has_any ("generateEcCert", "packageUserSize", "cert_action_entry")
| extend ApiFunc = case(AdditionalFields has "generateEcCert", "generateEcCert", AdditionalFields has "packageUserSize", "packageUserSize", "cert_action_entry_geneccert")
| summarize ConcurrentCalls = count(), DistinctApis = dcount(ApiFunc), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5s)
| where ConcurrentCalls >= 7
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert", "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize") or (SyslogMessage has "cert_action_entry" and SyslogMessage has "geneccert")
| extend User = coalesce(extract(@"cpanel_jsonapi_user=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage), extract(@"cpanel_jsonuser=([^&\s]+)", 1, SyslogMessage))
| extend SrcIp = extract(@"((?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ApiFunc = case(SyslogMessage has "generateEcCert", "generateEcCert", SyslogMessage has "packageUserSize", "packageUserSize", "cert_action_entry_geneccert")
| summarize ConcurrentCalls = count(), DistinctApis = dcount(ApiFunc), CallTypes = make_set(ApiFunc), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, User, SrcIp, bin_time = bin(TimeGenerated, 5s)
| where ConcurrentCalls between (7 .. 20) // LiteSpeed-published exploit signature: 7-10 concurrent calls per attempt
| order by bin_time desc
source:linux.syslog ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert" OR "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize" OR ("cert_action_entry" "geneccert"))
#event_simpleName=/^(ProcessRollup2|SyntheticProcessRollup2)$/ | CommandLine=/cpanel_jsonapi_func=(generateEcCert|packageUserSize)/i OR CommandLine=/cert_action_entry.*geneccert/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, bucket=1s], function=count(as=concurrent_calls)) | concurrent_calls >= 7 | concurrent_calls <= 20
APPLICATION

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 7 AND count <= 20
| stats max(count) as peak_concurrent sum(count) as total_calls values(user) as users earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen by dest src
| where peak_concurrent >= 7
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.uri_query="*cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert*" OR Web.uri_query="*cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize*" OR Web.uri_query="*cert_action_entry*geneccert*") by _time Web.dest Web.src Web.user span=2s

| where count >= 7 AND count <= 20

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'

level: high
